chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern (longitudinal attrition not applicable; minimal cross-sectional item missingness). Because the NSS waves are independent cross-sections rather than a panel following the same slums over time (p. 29), longitudinal attrition does not apply; within the 10-state sample, complete-case restriction excluded only 21 of 2,411 slums (0.87%, leaving n = 2,390; p. 6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High / Serious concern for causal inference (Some concern for associational inference). Multilevel and fixed-effects regressions adjust for state effects, survey wave, slum household count (linear and quadratic), land ownership, fringe vs. central location, surrounding land use, and community association presence (pp. 10-11, Tables 5 and A4). However, the repeated cross-sectional design cannot rule out reverse causation (less-deprived or politically organized slums securing notification, p. 29; or prior improvement aid reducing 2012 BSDS in Regression 2, pp. 11-12) or unmeasured household- and city-level confounders (migrant recency, household income/wealth, caste, municipal fiscal capacity).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality. Legal exposure captures formal government recognition ('notified' vs. 'non-notified' slum status) and notification duration ('years notified', modeled with linear and quadratic terms as well as a binary indicator in Table A1), complemented by public/central/private land-jurisdiction categories (pp. 10-12, 28). Key limitations are community-level homogeneity assumptions (masking household-level cutoff-date tenure rules in cities such as Mumbai, pp. 29-30), pooling heterogeneous state notification regimes without statutory disaggregation, and unreported NSS field verification procedures for years notified.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some / Moderate concern. Both legal status (notified vs. non-notified and years notified) and service/funding outcomes are measured at the aggregate slum settlement level describing the 'majority of residents' rather than individual households (pp. 5-6, 29-30), obscuring intra-slum heterogeneity. The manuscript also does not report how NSS enumerators verified notification duration or 2012 government scheme receipt (e.g., official municipal records vs. local informant recall).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality. Basic water and sanitation services are operationalized using concrete NSSO settlement-level infrastructure indicators—drinking water source (tap, tubewell/handpump, well/other), latrine type (septic/flush/pour-flush, service/pit/public, none), underground sewer, covered/open drainage, monsoon waterlogging, and municipal solid waste collection (Table 1, p. 7)—reported separately (Table 3, p. 15) and combined into the Basic Services Deprivation Score (BSDS), whose weighting is validated across expert weights, polychoric factor analysis (Table A2), and NFHS-3 infant-mortality regression weights (Table A3). Limitations include majority-resident settlement coding without household coverage rates, water quality/continuity, or latrine-sharing metrics, and unverified informant reporting for 2012 JNNURM/RAY aid.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low to Some concern. No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported (standard for secondary observational NSS analyses), leaving discretionary choices such as BSDS category cutpoints (<=30, 31-60, >60 in Regression 2; p. 12) unverified against prior specification. However, transparency is strong: the authors report minor NSSO replication discrepancies (p. 6), present individual component trends alongside composite scores (Table 3), and provide four full sensitivity models in Appendix Tables A1-A4.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern. The study draws on four nationally representative NSS urban slum rounds (1993, 2002, 2008-09, 2012; n = 2,901 slums) that explicitly sample non-notified as well as notified slums, avoiding Census undercounting of unrecognized settlements (p. 5). Analytic restriction to the 10 states with >=10 sampled slums per wave is clearly justified and retains 83.1% of sampled slums (2,411/2,901) with <0.9% complete-case loss (2,390/2,411; p. 6). However, exact NSSO operational criteria for classifying unnotified settlements as slums across rounds are not detailed in the paper (estimated total slums drop sharply in 2012 in Table 2), and demolition/relocation of non-notified slums over time (p. 28) may induce compositional survivor bias across waves.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors clearly define the analytic inclusion criteria: urban slums sampled in four waves of India's National Sample Survey—49th (1993), 58th (2002), 65th (2008-2009), and 69th (2012) rounds (N = 2,901)—restricted for regression and primary descriptive analyses to the 10 states with at least 10 sampled slums in every survey wave (n = 2,411) and complete non-missing data on model variables (n = 2,390 across all waves; n = 706 in the 2012 wave for Regression Analysis 2).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6, Section 2(i); PDF Page 11, Section 2(iv); PDF Page 13, Table 2

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The unit of analysis (entire urban slum settlements in India), the 10 included states (Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Delhi, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal), survey years (1993-2012), unweighted and weighted slum and household counts, land ownership types, central vs. fringe city locations, surrounding land uses, and community association prevalence are thoroughly documented.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6, Section 2(i); PDF Pages 13, 15, 20-21, Tables 2, 3, and 5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposure is slum legal status ('notified' vs. 'non-notified' and continuous 'years notified') from the NSS urban slum surveys. While NSS is the sole national survey capturing slum legal status, the paper provides no details on how field enumerators verified notification status or exact duration of notification (e.g., official gazette/municipal records vs. informant recall over multiple decades), and explicitly notes that NSS assigns a single slum-wide legal status even where household-level recognition varies within settlements (such as cutoff-date tenure rules in Mumbai).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6, Section 2(i); PDF Pages 10-12, Sections 2(iii)-(iv); PDF Pages 29-30, Section 4(iv)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the study uses standardized national NSSO slum survey rounds and replicates official NSSO descriptive counts within 0.04%-2%, the manuscript does not state the specific operational criteria NSSO enumerators used to define and bound a 'slum' settlement (particularly non-notified slums) or explain whether NSSO slum definitions remained uniform across the 1993, 2002, 2008-09, and 2012 rounds (notably, Table 2 shows estimated national slums falling from 48,994 in 2008 to 33,510 in 2012 while sampled slum households rose fivefold).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-6, Section 1 and Section 2(i); PDF Page 13, Table 2

domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly identify key settlement- and state-level confounders—state policy environments, land ownership jurisdiction (state/city, central government, private), slum population size (households), city location (fringe vs. central), surrounding area type (residential, commercial, industrial), community association presence, and secular time trends (survey year)—as well as unmeasured confounders in the Discussion (recent migrant sorting, household financial resources, and collective efficacy).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-5, Section 1; PDF Pages 10-11, Section 2(iii); PDF Pages 28-29, Sections 4(iii)-(iv)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Strategies to address observed confounders are clearly stated and implemented via multivariable multilevel linear and logistic regressions nesting slums within states (random intercepts), controlling for survey wave fixed effects, quadratic functional forms for slum household size, land ownership, fringe/central location, surrounding area, and community associations, plus a state fixed-effects sensitivity model (Table A4). Residual unmeasured confounding and reverse causality remain inherent limitations of the cross-sectional data and are transparently acknowledged.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 9-12, Sections 2(ii)-(iv); PDF Pages 20-25, Tables 5-6; PDF Pages 40-41, Table A4

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: The primary outcome (12-item Basic Services Deprivation Score, BSDS) is built from concrete NSSO infrastructure items and rigorously checked across three weighting schemes (literature-based health weights, polychoric factor analysis, and NFHS-3 infant-mortality regression weights). Nevertheless, the paper does not report NSSO field ascertainment methods (direct inspection vs. key-informant interview) for either the 12 service indicators or the 2012 JNNURM/RAY financial aid question, and settlement-level majority coding masks within-slum household heterogeneity in water and sanitation access.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-12, Sections 2(i)-(iv); PDF Page 7, Table 1; PDF Pages 29-30, Section 4(iv); PDF Pages 38-40, Tables A2-A3

domain_ratings.justification: The authors apply survey weights to descriptive and multivariable estimates, model state-level clustering via multilevel linear and logistic regressions (with Goldstein-Healy multiple-comparison adjustments) alongside a state fixed-effects specification (given the small number of state clusters, K = 10), include statistically justified quadratic terms, compute Cohen's f-squared variance contributions, and confirm robustness across four sensitivity models. A secondary caveat in Regression Analysis 2 is conditioning on contemporaneous 2012 BSDS when modeling prior receipt of slum improvement funds, as past aid could itself lower 2012 deprivation.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 6, 9-12, Section 2; PDF Pages 20-25, Tables 5-6; PDF Pages 37-41, Tables A1-A4

overall_narrative_summary: Overall methodological judgment: Some concern (JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional Studies checklist: 5 Yes [Q1, Q2, Q5, Q6, Q8], 3 Unclear [Q3, Q4, Q7], 0 No). This repeated cross-sectional analysis of 2,390 slums across 10 major Indian states in four National Sample Survey (NSS) waves (1993, 2002, 2008-09, 2012) exhibits substantial analytical rigor for an observational secondary survey study: unlike the Indian Census, the NSS samples both notified and non-notified slums; complete-case missingness within the 10-state analytic sample is under 1% (21/2,411 slums); multivariable regressions adjust for state random or fixed effects, survey year, slum population size, land ownership jurisdiction, central vs. fringe location, surrounding land use, and community associations; and findings remain consistent across four sensitivity specifications testing binary vs. continuous legal status and factor-analytic or NFHS-3 mortality-derived Basic Services Deprivation Score (BSDS) weights. Methodological concerns center on (1) non-causal repeated cross-sectional structure, leaving serious vulnerability to reverse causation (better-serviced or politically organized settlements securing notification; or prior improvement grants altering 2012 BSDS in Regression Analysis 2) and unmeasured household socioeconomic/migrant confounding; (2) ecological settlement-level ('majority of residents') measurement, which obscures intra-slum household heterogeneity in legal recognition and water/sanitation access; and (3) lack of reporting in the paper on NSSO operational criteria for defining unnotified slums across waves and field verification protocols for notification duration and government scheme funding.
study_design_identified: Repeated cross-sectional observational study (pooled multilevel linear regression across four cross-sectional waves of India's National Sample Survey [1993, 2002, 2008-09, 2012] and single-wave multilevel logistic regression [2012] at the slum settlement level)
where_found_summary: Methods and sample construction on PDF Pages 5-12 (Section 2, Table 1); descriptive and multivariable results on PDF Pages 12-25 (Section 3, Tables 2-6, Figures 1-3); methodological limitations (non-longitudinal cross-sectional design, reverse causation, unmeasured confounding, settlement-level ecological aggregation) on PDF Pages 29-30 (Section 4(iv)); sensitivity models on PDF Pages 37-41 (Appendix Tables A1-A4).
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes four independent repeated cross-sectional waves of National Sample Survey slum-settlement data using observational multivariable linear and logistic regressions without following individual slums longitudinally and without a quasi-experimental intervention/comparator design (no DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, or ITS; the authors explicitly state on p. 29 that the NSS does not follow the same slums longitudinally and is not designed to establish causality). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression studies without a quasi-experimental intervention structure map to the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.
